title: The Benefits (and Perils) of Thinking Hard
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson works through a subtle problem hiding inside Dan Willingham's famous line 'memory is the residue of thought': if hard thinking produces learning, and retrieval practice works precisely because it demands harder thinking than review, then students who believe hard thinking signals failure will actively avoid the very effort that helps them learn. Citing a recent meta-analysis finding that perceived mental effort is consistently negatively correlated with perceived learning, Watson shows this false belief is not hypothetical -- students genuinely do experience effortful thinking as both unpleasant and as evidence they don't understand the material. His three classroom recommendations are: tell students directly and repeatedly that hard thinking is a sign of learning, not failure; show them the research evidence (for instance framing it as a retrieval-vs-rereading comparison question); and use sports or arts analogies, since most students already accept without question that repetitive, effortful practice is simply what getting better at anything requires.
points: Watson's key move is connecting two separate ideas that are usually discussed apart -- 'memory is the residue of thought' and the research finding that effort predicts *lower* perceived learning -- to expose a hidden trap in the case for retrieval practice.

The meta-analysis finding that perceived effort and perceived learning are negatively correlated on average means students are systematically misreading their own hardest, most productive thinking as evidence of failure.

His three-part response (tell them directly, show them the research, use sport/arts analogies) escalates from simple assertion to evidence to relatable analogy, giving teachers layered tools depending on the audience and moment.

The framing that 'that feeling... this is really complicated... is you learning the concept' gives teachers a specific, repeatable phrase to counter students' in-the-moment discouragement during effortful tasks.
quotes: In that book -- one of the first to make cognitive science clear and practical for classroom teachers -- Willingham wrote this immortal sentence: "Memory is the residue of thought.
Well, because students have to think harder when they retrieve than when they review. And because they think harder, they remember more.
If our students believe that hard thinking is proof that they didn't learn, they face two compelling reasons not to think hard.
The amount of mental effort experienced during a learning task is usually negatively correlated with learners' perception of learning.
That feeling in your head right now…that feeling 'this is really complicated!' … that feeling is you learning the concept.
In every case, the need for all this hard work isn't a sign that you can't dance/score/act; instead, it's a perfectly normal part of getting better at dancing, scoring, and acting.
